title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 33-40
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 33-40 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A trigger runs a SOQL query once for every record in the batch. Why does this design break under a large data load?
options: Query cost scales with record count while the budget does not.
Each query resets the transaction budget for the next one, so cost stays flat.
The row limit is reached long before the statement limit is reached.
Queries issued inside a trigger each consume an extra DML statement.
questions.explanation: A per-record query makes resource use grow with the batch size while the transaction budget stays fixed; binding the whole collection in one query keeps cost proportional to distinct objects touched.

questions.question: A single DML operation inserts 1,000 records and fires a trigger on that object. How often does the trigger code execute?
options: Once per record, each one running with a full transaction budget.
Once per batch of 200 records, each firing as its own transaction.
Once for the entire load, because one DML statement is one transaction.
Twice, once before the database write and once after the commit.
questions.explanation: Triggers run on batches of 200 records, so a larger load fires the trigger several times, and each firing is a fresh transaction with its own governor budget.

questions.question: An object has four separate triggers, each querying the same related records. What is the problem and the recommended fix?
options: Each trigger keeps its own governor budget, so separating them improves isolation.
All logic should move into the trigger file so that nothing is shared across files.
They share one budget and fire unordered; use one trigger per object that routes to a handler.
Multiple triggers are safe whenever each one stays short, readable, and clearly named for its purpose.
questions.explanation: Multiple triggers on one object draw from the same budget and have no guaranteed firing order; a single thin trigger per object that delegates restores ordered execution and predictable budget use.

questions.question: A custom object must reference an Account, an Opportunity, or a Case, and all three already relate to one Account. What is the sound modeling choice?
options: Add a custom polymorphic field that can point at any of the three objects.
Point the record at the shared Account as a normal lookup.
Create three separate versions of the object, one for each parent type.
Store the parent type and the parent Id in two separate text fields.
questions.explanation: When the candidate parents share a meaningful common ancestor, pointing at the ancestor turns a wild polymorphic field into a normal, reportable, securable lookup that every query and report can handle.

questions.question: Two subtypes of one concept share almost no fields or relationships. Why is one object with record types a poor fit?
options: Record types cannot be reported on across all subtypes in one place.
Record types cannot give each subtype its own layout, picklist values, or required fields.
Record types hide fields from the user, not the database.
Record types prevent an object from having a sharing and security model.
questions.explanation: A record type only hides a field from the user, never from the database, so deeply divergent subtypes pile meaningless fields onto one object; separate objects behind a shared supertype fit better.

questions.question: What does a roll-up summary field require and cost in exchange for showing a parent aggregate without an aggregate query?
options: A master-detail relationship plus write cost on the parent per child change.
A lookup relationship and manual refresh whenever the aggregate should update.
No stored value and a recomputation of the aggregate on every read.
Indexable storage that offsets its cost by making filters faster.
questions.explanation: A roll-up summary is platform-maintained denormalization: it needs a master-detail relationship and adds write work on the parent each time a child changes, in return for a cached aggregate on read.

questions.question: A coverage rule says an incident on a lapsed policy is not covered, and it depends on policy status, coverage dates, and the incident date together. Where should the rule live?
options: In the agent's prompt, so the model can reason about the policy language.
Split across the tools that expose each field, so each one enforces its part.
In the output schema, which validates the shape of the model's response.
In the aggregate behind its root, decided together in one place.
questions.explanation: An aggregate is a consistency boundary: anything that must stay true together is read and decided behind the aggregate root, not assembled from separate sources in free text.

questions.question: A team is about to draw an agent graph for a new system. What should be established first?
options: The agent graph, because the available tools determine the responsibilities.
The bounded contexts and their shared language, since agents follow the model.
The prompt library, because the vocabulary inside each prompt defines the boundaries.
One all-purpose agent, split later only if its performance suffers.
questions.explanation: Agents are an implementation detail; the context map comes first, or the agent graph reproduces whatever tools happened to be available instead of the shape of the business.

questions.question: How should a domain system treat a state change proposed by a model?
options: As an authorized decision once the output schema accepts it as valid.
As a trusted instruction to execute immediately against stored state.
As an untrusted proposal the domain must authorize before executing.
As free text that a human reviewer must approve before any change is applied.
questions.explanation: A schema validates shape but cannot enforce meaning, so model output is an untrusted proposal that deterministic domain code must normalize, authorize, and then execute through the aggregate.

questions.question: An org changes a high-volume object's default access from Private to Read Only. What does the platform do?
options: Flips the flag instantly and leaves existing share records untouched.
Runs a background recalculation that adds and removes share records to match.
Deletes every manual share on the object and requires each one to be rebuilt.
Rebuilds the role hierarchy so it matches the new default access level.
questions.explanation: Changing an org-wide default starts a sharing recalculation that adds new share records and removes redundant ones, so on a large object it is a scheduled event with a maintenance window.

questions.question: A user who can see an Opportunity can also see its parent Account, though no rule or share record was created. What explains this?
options: A sharing rule opened the Account to that user.
The account hierarchy rolled access up from the opportunity.
Parent implicit sharing for standard parent-child pairs.
A manual share created automatically by the opportunity owner.
questions.explanation: Implicit sharing is native and cannot be turned off: seeing a child opportunity, case, contact, or order grants access to the associated account, without any rule or share record.

questions.question: Some users can see records that should be private, and no share record explains the extra access. Which declarative mechanism narrows access?
options: A stricter sharing rule written against the same records and users.
Apex managed sharing with a new sharing reason attached.
A lower org-wide default applied without running a recalculation pass.
A restriction rule, which filters records rather than opening access.
questions.explanation: Sharing rules and manual shares only open access, so the tool that narrows visibility is a restriction rule, which filters the records a user can see.

questions.question: A nightly job must process tens of thousands of records in chunks, keep a running total, and pick up failures on the next run. Which primitive and pattern fit?
options: A single future method that iterates every record, since it gets its own transaction.
One queueable job per record, so each record's retry is isolated on its own.
A scheduled class that performs the work directly, since scheduled code is async.
Batch Apex with a stateful counter, started by a schedulable, plus a retry flag.
questions.explanation: Batch Apex handles volume with chunk-level fault isolation, a stateful counter carries the total across chunks, and a flag on each record lets the next run pick up failures; the scheduler only starts it.

questions.question: A design enqueues one asynchronous job per record while iterating a large query. Why is this a problem?
options: Async capacity is a shared org-level budget, so cost scales with record count.
Each job runs in its own transaction, which is the safest option for isolation.
Async limits are allocated per feature, so one job per record cannot affect others.
Queueable jobs cannot accept sObjects, so the design will not compile at all.
questions.explanation: Asynchronous capacity is an org-level budget shared with every other feature, so a job per record multiplies the shared cost by the record count and hits the per-transaction enqueue cap.

questions.question: What is the correct job of a scheduled class?
options: Running heavy queries and callouts itself, since it runs asynchronously.
Holding the trigger time and handing off to a batch job or a queueable.
Carrying large record collections between runs using persisted instance state.
Replacing batch Apex entirely for any large-volume processing need.
questions.explanation: The scheduler answers when, not how: it runs under tight synchronous-style limits, so its body should hand off to a batch job or a queueable where the real work and higher budget live.

questions.question: A loop updates one record per iteration and fails at the 151st update. Which meter fired?
options: The DML row meter, which caps at 10,000 rows per transaction.
The query row meter, which caps at 50,000 returned rows.
The DML statement meter, at 150, while the row meter is barely used.
The SOQL statement meter, which caps at 100 queries per transaction.
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are independent meters, so per-record updates exhaust the 150-statement budget while the row meter has barely moved; batching into one call on a list fixes it.

questions.question: Moving a transaction to asynchronous execution raises which budgets?
options: All of them, including the DML row and SOQL row ceilings.
The query, heap, and CPU budgets, but not the DML or row limits.
Only the DML statement limit, which roughly doubles in async code.
None; asynchronous code is governed by the same limits as sync code.
questions.explanation: Async execution roughly doubles the query count and raises heap and CPU, but DML stays at 150 statements and 10,000 rows and SOQL rows stay at 50,000, so async alone will not save a DML-row failure.

questions.question: A save fires your trigger, a record-triggered flow, and an uncertified installed package. Whose budget do they spend?
options: Each of the three gets its own separate allocation.
Only the trigger and the flow share, because every package is isolated.
The package brings its own pool, because installed packages are certified.
One pool owned by the transaction, so headroom counts every consumer.
questions.explanation: Every process that fires on a save spends from one transaction budget, and only certified packages get their own pool, so a design review must leave headroom for automation you did not write.

questions.question: Where should a trigger set or normalize a field on the record being saved, and why?
options: In before context, where the change persists with no extra DML.
In after context, because the record already has an Id at that point.
In a separate DML update issued after the trigger finishes running.
In a validation rule, which modifies field values before the record writes.
questions.explanation: Values set on the in-memory record in before context are persisted by the same save with no separate DML statement, which keeps the transaction small.

questions.question: An after-update trigger reads a parent's roll-up summary field to make a decision. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; roll-up summaries are recalculated before after triggers run.
Roll-ups recalculate after after triggers, so the value is stale.
Roll-up summary fields cannot be read from Apex trigger code at all.
The trigger should read Trigger.old instead of the parent roll-up.
questions.explanation: Roll-up recalculation happens near the end of the save, well after after triggers, so an after trigger reading the roll-up sees the pre-recalculation value.

questions.question: A batch upserts 5,000 records, some new and some existing, in one transaction. Which save contexts run?
options: Only before insert and after insert, because upsert is treated as an insert.
Only before update and after update, because existing records dominate the set.
All four contexts, so the trigger must dispatch on the operation it faces.
No contexts run, because batch operations bypass record triggers.
questions.explanation: A transaction is not limited to one operation, so a mixed upsert runs before insert, before update, after insert, and after update, and the trigger must dispatch on the operation rather than assume one.

questions.question: What is the difference between context and memory in an agent?
options: Context survives beyond the window; memory is what is in the window now.
Context is what is in the window now; memory survives beyond it.
Context lives in the database; memory lives in the model's fixed weights.
They are the same thing, measured in different units of time.
questions.explanation: Context is the set of tokens in the window right now, while memory is the selective state retained across interactions and stored outside the model.

questions.question: Which task is best served by a stateless design?
options: A long-running support workflow that spans many days.
A coding assistant that must recall earlier design decisions.
One-shot classification where each request is independent.
An agent that resumes a complex claim across separate sessions.
questions.explanation: Extraction, classification, and one-shot calls are independent requests with no continuity to keep, so statelessness keeps them simple and easy to scale.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a memory layer to the question it answers?
options: Semantic memory answers what happened; episodic memory answers what is true.
Procedural memory stores domain facts; semantic memory stores routines.
Working memory stores durable facts; long-term memory holds the window.
Semantic memory is what is true; episodic memory is what happened.
questions.explanation: Semantic memory holds durable facts about what is true, while episodic memory records time-indexed experiences and answers what happened.
